Scornful means feeling or showing scorn — a powerful mix of contempt and superiority directed at someone or something you see as worthless, foolish, or beneath you. A scornful person doesn't just dislike something. They look at it and feel it is so low, so unworthy, that it barely deserves serious attention. There is always a sense of looking down built into this word.

To put it plainly: disapproval says "I don't agree with this." Scorn says "I can't believe this even exists."
The Feeling Behind It

When someone is scornful, two things are happening at once inside them:

First, they feel contempt — a deep sense that someone or something is inferior or worthless.

Second, they feel superiority — a sense that they themselves are above it, that they stand higher and know better.

These two feelings together create scorn. It is not angry frustration (that would be rage). It is not simple dislike (that would be disapproval). Scorn is cooler, sharper, and more cutting — it is the feeling of someone who believes they are operating on a completely different and higher level than whatever they are reacting to.
How It Shows in Real Life

Scorn is rarely hidden. It has a very recognizable face. A scornful person might:

give a slow, dismissive laugh, as if the very idea being presented is a joke. Or they might sneer — that twisted half-smile that signals mockery. They might speak in a flat, cutting tone that makes the other person feel small and foolish. They might roll their eyes, sigh with exasperation, or deliver a sharp remark that puts someone firmly in their place. Even silence can be scornful — a cold, withering look that says more than words.

Notice that all of these express the same underlying message: you are beneath me.
The Strength of the Word

"Scornful" is a strong, loaded word. It sits at the sharp end of a scale:

Unimpressed → Critical → Dismissive → Scornful

Someone who is merely dismissive might shrug and walk away. Someone who is critical will point out flaws. But someone who is scornful communicates contempt — they don't just disagree with you, they look down on you for your position, your ability, or your choices. Scorn carries a sting. It is designed, consciously or not, to diminish.
What People Are Scornful Of

You can be scornful of almost anything — people, ideas, behaviors, beliefs, or things. Common uses include:

scornful of weakness (treating any show of vulnerability as pathetic), scornful of wealth (looking down on material ambition as vulgar), scornful of ignorance (treating people who know less as unworthy of respect), or scornful of someone's efforts (viewing their attempt as laughably inadequate).

The word "of" is its natural companion: you are always scornful of something or someone.
Example Sentences

These will help you see the word alive in different contexts:

"She gave him a scornful glance when he suggested she was not capable of leading the team."

"He was scornful of anyone who had not read widely, and made sure they knew it."

"The critic was scornful of the film, calling it childish and beneath serious discussion."

"There was a scornful smile on her lips as he fumbled through his excuses."

"He spoke in a scornful tone that made everyone in the room feel small and foolish."

"She waved away the suggestion with a scornful laugh."

In each of these, notice the consistent thread: someone is not just unimpressed — they are looking down.
How It Describes Different Things

"Scornful" can describe a wide range of things:

A look ("a scornful look"), a laugh ("a scornful laugh"), a tone ("a scornful tone of voice"), a remark ("a scornful comment"), or a person's entire attitude ("she was scornful of everyone around her"). This makes it a flexible and very expressive word.
Other Forms of the Word

Scornfully (adverb) — describes how something is done: "She scornfully rejected his offer."

Scorn (noun) — the feeling itself: "He looked at the painting with scorn."

Scorn (verb) — to treat something with contempt: "She scorned his advice and did the opposite."

Scornfulness (noun) — the quality or state of being scornful: "His scornfulness made it hard to work with him."
Words Close in Meaning (and How They Differ)

Contemptuous is the closest word to scornful. Both involve looking down on someone. The subtle difference is that contemptuous tends to focus on the internal feeling, while scornful is more often about the expression of that feeling — the outward display.

Disdainful is similar but often colder and quieter. A disdainful person considers something beneath them and simply refuses to engage. A scornful person is more likely to express that feeling openly — with a sneer, a remark, or a laugh.

Derisive leans more toward outright mockery and laughter. Scorn can be silent and cold; derision is almost always loud and mocking.

Dismissive means treating something as not worth your time, but without necessarily the superior contempt that scornful always carries.
The Opposite
The natural opposites of scornful are respectful (treating someone as worthy), admiring (viewing someone positively), and reverent (approaching something with deep respect or awe).
The Big Picture

To lock in the meaning permanently: imagine the expression on the face of someone who has just been shown something they consider laughably beneath them — something foolish, weak, or inferior. That face — that mixture of contempt, superiority, and dismissal — is the face of a scornful person. The word always lives at this intersection: you are less than me, and I want you to know it.
